paragraph: The government agency IMA issued [terms of reference on 9 February 2026](<https://sys.portais.gov.ao/uploads/Td_R_Consultoria_para_Implementacao_da_Interoperabilidade_da_Administracao_Publica_1_13f0252ef0.pdf>) reporting that a seven-month study with 25 public institutions produced a Framework and Roadmap of Interoperability for the public administration. The framework carries organisational, semantic, technical and infrastructure guidelines. It dates from the last twelve months, and no earlier position has been found. [The same study](<https://sys.portais.gov.ao/uploads/Td_R_Consultoria_para_Implementacao_da_Interoperabilidade_da_Administracao_Publica_1_13f0252ef0.pdf>) found that the institutions shared no common standards. The document names no instrument adopting the framework. Establishing would need standards issued that set the data formats, codes, interfaces or protocols government systems must use.

Benin's interoperability framework was [published by the digital agency ASIN and instituted by decree 2020-209 of 18 March 2020](<https://api.xroad.bj/documents/10/download>). It names the technical standards government systems are to use. They include W3C web service and XML standards, the ODF document format and the JPEG and PNG image formats. In the last twelve months, [a legal note from ASIN in July 2026](<https://asin.bj/doc/142/download>) treated the framework as in place. [A consultation workshop in Cotonou on 30 June 2026](<https://lanation.bj/actualites/transformation-numerique-de-letat-un-cadre-commun-pour-ses-systemes-dinformation-en-preparation>) examined a draft policy that sets technical rules and standards for public systems. No source found says a law, decree, regulation or circular requires public bodies to use the standards. Operating would need a law, decree, regulation or circular making them compulsory for the systems public bodies build or buy.

Burkina Faso's general interoperability referential was [adopted by order of the Prime Minister on 23 May 2018](<https://burkina24.com/2019/10/15/burkina-un-referentiel-pour-moderniser-ladministration-publique/>). [The decree on the public administration's digital platforms](<https://lefaso.net/IMG/pdf/decret_portant_modalite_de_mise_en_exploitation_des_plateformes_numeriques_de_l_administration_publique.pdf>), published by August 2024, makes a favourable opinion a condition of putting a platform into service. The file submitted for that opinion includes a check that the platform respects the referential. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found from the last three years names a public body, system or product tested, audited or certified against the standards. Mature would need a dated source naming a public body, system or product checked against them, or giving a count.

[Expertise France's project page of 17 February 2026](<https://www.expertisefrance.fr/en/projects/digital-transformation-botswana>) says its project, funded by the European Union and running from August 2024 to August 2027, works with ESTDEV to improve and align Botswana's national interoperability framework, standards, guidelines and tools. The page lists a harmonised and operational national interoperability framework for e-government services as an expected result. It does not say the framework has been adopted or issued. The page dates from the last twelve months, and no earlier position has been found. No source found says the standards have been published. Establishing would need standards issued that set the data formats, codes, interfaces or protocols government systems must use.

Côte d'Ivoire's general interoperability referential is [annexed to decree 2021-913 of 22 December 2021](<https://anssi.gouv.ci/documents/28/décret_2021-913_du_22_décembre_2021_adoption_référentiel_général_dinteropérabilité_systèmes_dinformation.pdf>), which adopts it. It lists reference standards for network and messaging protocols, SOAP and REST web services, and data formats and encodings including XML, JSON, XSD, PDF/A and UTF-8. [Article 3 of the decree](<https://anssi.gouv.ci/documents/28/décret_2021-913_du_22_décembre_2021_adoption_référentiel_général_dinteropérabilité_systèmes_dinformation.pdf>) says public bodies are bound to conform to the referential. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found from the last three years names a public body, system or product tested, audited or certified against the standards. Mature would need a dated source naming a public body, system or product checked against them, or giving a count.

[A ministry workshop on 2 and 3 February 2022](<https://medd.gouv.cd/atelier-sur-lelaboration-et-adoption-des-referentiels-numeriques-du-secteur-public-en-rdc/>) validated five books of digital standards for the public sector. Among them is a general interoperability framework meant to let public information systems exchange data in real time. [The government adopted the draft digital norms and standards on 15 April 2022](<https://kt.cd/2022/04/16/adoption-du-projet-des-normes-et-standards-du-numerique-applicable-au-secteur-public/>), in the same five books. [The report of the April 2022 adoption](<https://kt.cd/2022/04/16/adoption-du-projet-des-normes-et-standards-du-numerique-applicable-au-secteur-public/>) says legal force was still to be given to the standards by ministerial order. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says the standards have been published. Establishing would need standards issued that set the data formats, codes, interfaces or protocols government systems must use.

[Version 2.0 of the eGovernment Interoperability Framework](<https://nita.gov.gh/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Ghana-eGovernment-Interoperability-Framework-eGIF-Version-2.0_v.Draft-for-Stakeholder-Review-1.pdf>), from the National Information Technology Agency and dated 2022 by its publication, is labelled a draft for stakeholder review. Its technical annexes set standards for government systems on the interoperability of data, networks, service-oriented architecture, channels, business processes, security and applications. It updates the framework the agency adopted in 2008, the government's first. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says the standards have been published. Establishing would need standards issued that set the data formats, codes, interfaces or protocols government systems must use.

No stage is set. The one source found on Guinea's interoperability rules is a page dated only 2026, after the assessment date of 10 November 2026. Nothing dated earlier says the rules are published or being written. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source dated in the last three years says the country has no technical standards for its systems to exchange data. Preparing would need a named set of technical standards for government systems to exchange data shown to be drafted or out for consultation.

Guinea-Bissau's National Regulation on Interoperability of Digital Systems and Platforms was [published in the Boletim Oficial on 31 October 2025 as Decree 27/2025](<https://wardip.gw/governo-aprova-regulamento-nacional-de-interoperabilidade-para-acelerar-a-transformacao-digital-na-guine-bissau/>). The digital integration programme WARDIP reported the decree. Among the regulation's objectives it lists the establishment of technical standards for developing interoperable digital solutions and the harmonising of communication between systems. The report does not list the standards themselves. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says a law, decree, regulation or circular requires public bodies to use the standards. Operating would need a law, decree, regulation or circular making them compulsory for the systems public bodies build or buy.

[The ICT Authority's second edition of the Government Enterprise Architecture and Government Interoperability Framework](<https://cms.icta.go.ke/sites/default/files/2024-07/GEA%20-%20GIF%202nd%20Edition.pdf>), dated 2023, sets out an interoperability charter and data, technical and metadata standards for exchanging data between government agencies. Its approval date and document history are blank. [At a workshop with ministries, departments and agencies on 6 and 7 November 2025](<https://kdeap.icta.go.ke/kenya-advances-digital-government-gea-interoperability-workshop-held-at-kicc/>), the Authority said it would develop and finalise the national enterprise architecture standards and the interoperability framework. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says the standards have been published. Establishing would need standards issued that set the data formats, codes, interfaces or protocols government systems must use.

[A paper published on 30 June 2026](<https://cjos.histr.edu.ly/index.php/journal/en/article/view/2167>) sets out a national government interoperability platform, which it calls Nawa. Its abstract says that Libyan government institutions lack unified interoperability standards and that their information systems are fragmented. In November 2026 [an analysts' study found government data spread across several bodies without unified standards](<https://alwasat.ly/news/485548>). It recommended a national interoperability framework with binding standards. Both date from the last twelve months, and no earlier position has been found. No source found says whether standards are being written. Preparing would need a named set of technical standards for government systems to exchange data being drafted or out for consultation.

No stage is set. [A World Bank report counted eight systems compliant with the digital governance unit standards in October 2023](<https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099122123130031407/pdf/P1694131558e640e51a145152595653587b.pdf>), without saying what the standards are. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says Madagascar has published its interoperability standards or made them compulsory. No source found says they were drafted. Establishing would need the government or its standards body to issue the data formats, codes, interfaces or protocols its systems must use.

Mozambique's Electronic Government Systems Interoperability Regulation sets standards for integrating and managing public information systems, [the chairman of the national ICT institute INTIC said in a report of 5 December 2025](<https://techafricanews.com/2025/12/05/mozambique-prioritizes-data-governance-as-cornerstone-of-digital-sovereignty/>). In the last twelve months, he announced that a review of the regulation was complete. [Ecofin Agency reported on 24 September 2026](<https://www.ecofinagency.com/news-digital/2409-59214-mozambique-plans-unified-digital-public-services-platform-by-2029>) that the country was revising its 2017 interoperability framework. [On 23 October 2026 INTIC presented a proposed revision of Decree 67/2017](<https://pt.linkedin.com/posts/intic-instituto-nacional-de-tecnologias-de-informa%C3%A7%C3%A3o-e-comunica%C3%A7%C3%A3o_revis%C3%A3o-do-quadro-de-interoperabilidade-refor%C3%A7a-activity-7520792996766699521-sTTA>), which had not been adopted. No source found says a law, decree, regulation or circular requires public bodies to use the standards. Operating would need a law, decree, regulation or circular making them compulsory for the systems public bodies build or buy.

[The digital transformation ministry held a three-day workshop, reported on 27 March 2026](<https://techafricanews.com/2026/03/27/mauritania-moves-to-standardize-public-digital-services-with-national-framework-initiative/>), to develop a unified framework of standards for public digital services. It presented a technical study and a mechanism for putting the framework into effect, and asked for stakeholders' comments before full adoption. [GovStack says a government architecture standard for interoperability and security was put to a national consultation in March 2026](<https://govstack.global/news/build-once-use-across-government-mauritanias-govstack-journey/>). Both date from the last twelve months, and no earlier position has been found. No source found says the standards have been published. Establishing would need standards issued that set the data formats, codes, interfaces or protocols government systems must use.

Mauritius issued [version 1.0 of its e-Government Interoperability Framework in November 2002](<https://cib.govmu.org/Documents/Maintenance%20Agreement/egiframework.pdf>). The framework sets technical standards and specifications for interoperability across the government's information systems, and for the exchange of data between public agencies. It is the Government of Mauritius's own document. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says a law, decree, regulation or circular requires public bodies to use the standards. Operating would need a law, decree, regulation or circular making them compulsory for the systems public bodies build or buy.

[In September 2025 NITDA held a stakeholders' review of the draft Technical Standard for Nigeria Data Exchange](<https://thenationonlineng.net/fg-to-begin-implementation-of-digital-public-infrastructure-data-exchange-standards/>), known as NGDX. The Nigeria Governors Forum was among the reviewers, so that states and local governments could align with it. [NITDA's Director General said implementation of the standard could begin in the first quarter of 2026](<https://thenationonlineng.net/fg-to-begin-implementation-of-digital-public-infrastructure-data-exchange-standards/>), once the review was done. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says the data exchange standard has been issued, or that public bodies must use it. Establishing would need standards issued that set the data formats, codes, interfaces or protocols government systems must use.

[The digital ministry announced that on 5 May 2026](<https://fr.linkedin.com/posts/mctnsn_dpi-newdealtechnologique-activity-7457180609757528065-UqRT>) it would present the draft decree governing the interoperability platform and introduce the national interoperability framework, with its data-exchange architectures, technical standards and security requirements. Both the decree and the framework were at the stage of presentation. The draft decree had not been adopted at the announcement. The announcement dates from the last twelve months, and no earlier position has been found. No source found says the standards have been published. Establishing would need standards issued that set the data formats, codes, interfaces or protocols government systems must use.

[Lei 1/2024, passed by the National Assembly on 3 November 2023, promulgated on 30 November and gazetted on 29 January 2024](<https://inic.gov.st/viewdoc.php?id=26>), institutes the National Interoperability Framework (QNI). It applies to all public institutions. [The law grades each specification as mandatory or recommended](<https://inic.gov.st/viewdoc.php?id=26>). A mandatory item must be adopted in every new IT product or project. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found from the last three years names a public body, system or product tested, audited or certified against the specifications. Mature would need a dated source naming a public body, system or product checked against them, or giving a count.

Tanzania's e-Government Agency issued [version 1.0 of the e-Government Interoperability Framework: Standards and Technical Guidelines in February 2016](<https://www.ega.go.tz/uploads/standards/sw-1574945623-inter.pdf>). It sets nine areas of technical standards for government systems to exchange data, among them interconnection, data integration, metadata and security. [The communications ministry lists eGovernment Standards and Guidelines among its completed projects](<https://www.mawasiliano.go.tz/pages/completed-project>). No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says a law, decree, regulation or circular requires public bodies to use the standards. Operating would need a law, decree, regulation or circular making them compulsory for the systems public bodies build or buy.

[The national IT authority's e-Government Interoperability Framework, e-GIF-2026, dated 15 April 2026](<https://www.nita.go.ug/sites/default/files/2026-07/Uganda%20e-Government%20Interoperability%20Framework%20%28e-GIF%29-2026.pdf>), sets the prerequisites and guidelines for integrating government systems and sharing data across government. [Among its standards is DCAT for metadata, so that systems describe data the same way](<https://www.nita.go.ug/sites/default/files/2026-07/Uganda%20e-Government%20Interoperability%20Framework%20%28e-GIF%29-2026.pdf>). In the last twelve months, the authority dated this second national e-GIF 15 April 2026. The framework calls itself mandatory, which is the text speaking of itself. No law, decree, regulation or circular making the standards compulsory has been found. Operating would need a law, decree, regulation or circular making them compulsory for the systems public bodies build or buy.

The Department of Public Service and Administration [told Parliament on 28 August 2025](<https://pmg.org.za/committee-question/32258/>) that it had published the Minimum Interoperability Standards. In the last twelve months, [Operation Vulindlela's report of 31 July 2026](<https://www.treasury.gov.za/comm_media/press/2026/Operation%20Vulindlela%20Progress%20Report%20Q1%20-%202026.pdf>) says the standards were being updated between April and June 2026. The update was due to be tested in priority digital services by September 2026, and no source found says it has been issued. The 2023 Public Service Regulations [require each department's IT officer to ensure its systems interoperate](<https://pmg.org.za/committee-question/32258/>), without naming these standards. Operating would need public bodies to be required to use them.

Zambia's e-Government Division, the Smart Zambia Institute, issued [the Public Service ICT Electronic Government Interoperability Standard, first edition, in February 2019](<https://policyvault.africa/wp-content/uploads/policy/ZMB588.pdf>). The standard is meant to enable the exchange of data between the government information systems of different public bodies. It names data interoperability and technical interoperability guidelines within its scope. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says a law, decree, regulation or circular requires public bodies to use the standard. Operating would need a law, decree, regulation or circular making it compulsory for the systems public bodies build or buy.

A Herald column of November 2026 says the government is [building a whole-of-government enterprise architecture](<https://www.heraldonline.co.zw/transforming-public-services-through-one-digital-ecosystem/>). The column says the architecture defines interoperability standards, digital identity management, data governance and cybersecurity requirements. It names common data standards and secure application interfaces as what would let government systems communicate. It names no standard that has been issued. The column dates from the last twelve months, and no earlier position has been found. No source found says the standards have been issued, or that public bodies are required to use them. Establishing would need standards issued that set the data formats, codes, interfaces or protocols government systems must use.
